name: Battle of Kohima
info: A British and Indian garrison held Kohima ridge against the Japanese 31st Division in April 1944, was relieved, and with reinforcements drove the Japanese off, reopening the road to Imphal in June.

facts.date: 4 April to 22 June 1944, in three stages: the Japanese attack on Kohima ridge (3 to 16 April), the British and Indian counter-attack (18 April to 13 May) and the pursuit (16 May to 22 June)
facts.place: Kohima ridge and the surrounding hills, now the capital of Nagaland in north-east India, on the road between Dimapur and Imphal
facts.sides: British and British Indian forces, first the garrison under Colonel Hugh Richards (about 2,500, of whom about 1,000 were non-combatants) and then the British 2nd Division and Indian XXXIII Corps under Lieutenant General Montagu Stopford; the Japanese 31st Division under Lieutenant General Kōtoku Satō, part of Lieutenant General Renya Mutaguchi's Fifteenth Army
facts.outcome: The Japanese abandoned Kohima ridge in May and the Naga Village in late May, and on 22 June troops from Kohima and Imphal met at Milestone 109, ending the Siege of Imphal. British and Indian forces lost 4,064 men dead, missing and wounded; the Japanese lost at least 5,764 battle casualties in the Kohima area.

t: The Japanese 31st Division set out with only three weeks' supply of food and ammunition, and its lack of supplies was the decisive factor in the battle.

Fighting at the Deputy Commissioner's bungalow was so close that the tennis court became a no man's land with grenades thrown between trenches, and the Japanese were not driven from it until a tank was dragged up on 13 May.
Satō abandoned Naga Village on 31 May against Mutaguchi's orders, and the two commanders blamed each other afterwards.
dyk: The garrison's water supply point was on GPT Ridge and was captured by the Japanese on the first day of the siege; a small spring on Garrison Hill could be reached only at night.
ev: Imperial General Headquarters approves the U-Go offensive into India
The Japanese 31st Division crosses the Chindwin and spends six days fighting at Sangshak, which delays it by a week
The siege of Kohima begins and the garrison is driven into a small perimeter on Garrison Hill
Troops of 161st Indian Brigade with tanks break through and relieve the garrison
A tank dragged to the summit destroys the Japanese bunkers at the tennis court, clearing Kohima Ridge
Satō abandons Naga Village and the positions north of the road
Troops from Kohima and Imphal meet at Milestone 109, ending the Siege of Imphal
Satō is removed from command and the Japanese offensive is broken off

sections.background:
The Japanese plan to invade India, codenamed U-Go, was first meant as a spoiling attack on the British IV Corps at Imphal in Manipur, to disrupt Allied plans for 1944. Lieutenant General Renya Mutaguchi, commanding the Fifteenth Army, enlarged it into an invasion of India itself, perhaps even to overthrow the British Raj. A foothold in India would show the weakness of the British Empire and encourage Indian nationalists, and holding the area around Imphal would hurt American efforts to supply Chiang Kai-shek's army in China. Objections from various staffs were overcome and Imperial General Headquarters approved the offensive on 7 January 1944.

The plan sent the 31st Division to capture Kohima and so cut off Imphal. Mutaguchi wished to go on to Dimapur, the railhead and supply base in the Brahmaputra valley. The division's commander, Lieutenant General Kōtoku Satō, had not been involved in the planning and doubted that it could succeed; he had told his staff that they might all starve. He also thought Mutaguchi a blockhead, and the two had been on opposite sides in the Toseiha and Kodoha factions of the Japanese Army in the early 1930s.
sections.forces:
The 31st Division consisted of the 58th, 124th and 138th Infantry Regiments and the 31st Mountain Artillery Regiment. It crossed the Chindwin from 15 March on a front almost 60 miles (97 km) wide, and because of a shortage of transport it left behind half the mountain guns and the infantry's heavy weapons. It carried only three weeks' supply of food and ammunition. Its left wing, the bulk of the 58th Regiment under Major General Shigesaburō Miyazaki, was delayed by a week at Sangshak, where the 50th Indian Parachute Brigade lost 600 men and the Japanese over 400.

Lieutenant General William Slim, commanding the British Fourteenth Army, had believed that the terrain would allow the Japanese to send only a regiment to Kohima. Before 161st Indian Brigade arrived, the only fighting troops in the area were the newly raised 1st Battalion, Assam Regiment and a few platoons of the Assam Rifles. The garrison that held Kohima numbered about 2,500, of whom about 1,000 were non-combatants, under Colonel Hugh Richards. It included the 4th Battalion, Queen's Own Royal West Kent Regiment, a company of the 7th Rajput Regiment, a raw Nepalese battalion, the Shere Regiment, and convalescents and line-of-communication troops. The ridge runs north and south, with the Dimapur to Imphal road climbing to its northern end.
sections.course:
The siege began on 6 April. The garrison was shelled and mortared, partly with weapons and ammunition captured at Sangshak, and was driven into a small perimeter on Garrison Hill. The water supply point on GPT Ridge fell on the first day. The heaviest fighting was around the Deputy Commissioner's bungalow and tennis court, where the two sides dug in on opposite sides so close that grenades were thrown between the trenches. On the night of 17/18 April the Japanese took the bungalow area and Kuki Picquet, cutting the garrison in two, but did not attack Garrison Hill, being exhausted by hunger and fighting. On 18 April 161st Brigade, with tanks, broke through and began the relief, and the garrison handed over to 6th Brigade on 20 April.

The counter-offensive of the British 2nd Division was slow in monsoon mud against deeply dug, mutually supporting bunkers. Jail Hill, Kuki Picquet, FSD and DIS fell on 11 May, and on 13 May a Lee tank dragged up a bulldozed track destroyed the Japanese positions at the tennis court. Attacks on Naga Village and Aradura Spur on 24/25 and 28/29 May failed. On 31 May Satō abandoned Naga Village, and XXXIII Corps pushed south until it met the 5th Indian Division at Milestone 109 on 22 June.
sections.aftermath:
During the battle British and Indian forces lost 4,064 men, dead, missing and wounded. The Japanese lost at least 5,764 battle casualties in the Kohima area, and many of the 31st Division later died of disease or starvation, or took their own lives. Many were too weak to go further south than Ukhrul or Humine, where the hospitals had no medicines, staff or food.

Satō was removed from command early in July, when the whole Japanese offensive was broken off. He refused an invitation to commit seppuku and demanded a court martial to clear his name and publish his complaints about Fifteenth Army headquarters. At the prompting of Lieutenant General Masakasu Kawabe, commanding the Burma Area Army, he was declared to have suffered a mental breakdown and unfit to stand trial, and Lieutenant General Tsuchitaro Kawada replaced him. Miyazaki was promoted to command the 54th Division in Arakan. On the Allied side Major General John Grover was dismissed from the 2nd Division on 5 July for perceived slowness and after complaints about his handling of Indian formations, and Major General Cameron Nicholson replaced him. The Japanese losses at Imphal and Kohima, mainly from starvation and disease, crippled their defence of Burma against Allied attacks the following year.
sections.sources: One battle-hardened officer of 6th Brigade who saw the relieved garrison on 20 April described them as "aged, bloodstained scarecrows". Documents captured at Sangshak first showed Slim that a whole Japanese division was moving on Kohima. The Japanese commanders' conduct is disputed. Slim derided Satō as the most unenterprising of his opponents, while Japanese sources blame Mutaguchi for the weaknesses of the plan and for the antipathy between the two that led Satō to concentrate on saving his division. The Japanese loss is put at at least 5,764 battle casualties; later deaths from disease, starvation and suicide are not counted in it. The American historians Alan Millet and Williamson Murray wrote that nowhere in the Second World War, even on the Eastern Front, did the combatants fight with more mindless savagery.
sections.legacy:
The battle is called the turning point of the Japanese U-Go offensive. Martin Dougherty, Frank McLynn and Jonathan Ritter have called the battles of Kohima and Imphal the "Stalingrad of the East". Allied air supply was a major factor in turning the tide in this theatre, since garrisons could hold when surrounded and cut off, while the Japanese found their own supply harder to solve.

Three Victoria Crosses were awarded for actions at Kohima, to Lance Corporal John Pennington Harman of the Queen's Own Royal West Kent Regiment, Captain John Niel Randle of the Royal Norfolk Regiment and Jemadar Abdul Hafiz of the 9th Jat Regiment, at 18 the youngest recipient from the British Indian Army. The Kohima War Cemetery, holding 1,420 Allied war dead, lies on the slopes of Garrison Hill where the Deputy Commissioner's tennis court stood. The epitaph on the 2nd Division memorial, "When you go home, tell them of us and say, For your tomorrow, we gave our today", is attributed to John Maxwell Edmonds and thought to be inspired by Simonides' epitaph for Thermopylae. In 2024 the Nagaland Government and the Japanese ambassador unveiled the Kohima Peace Memorial.

summary: From April to June 1944 a British and Indian garrison at Kohima was besieged by the Japanese 31st Division, relieved, and then helped to drive it off the ridge. Short of food, the Japanese retreated, and the road to Imphal reopened on 22 June.
references: Fergal Keane, Road of Bones: The Siege of Kohima 1944 (HarperPress, 2010)
Leslie Edwards, Kohima: The Furthest Battle (The History Press, 2009)
John Colvin, Not Ordinary Men: The Story of the Battle of Kohima (Leo Cooper, 2012)
Louis Allen, Burma: The Longest War 1941–45 (Phoenix Press, 2000)
notes: The article gives no strength for the Japanese 31st Division, so none is given.
The article's text under Victoria Cross for Harman reads 'Detail Hill (FSD?)': left out. Randle's entry has no description in the article.
Kawabe is spelled 'Masakasu' as in the article (probably Masakazu).
The article's sources are thin: no contemporary accounts or archaeology are named; the sources section is short and rests on what the article attributes (Slim, Japanese sources, Millet and Murray).
Satō's rank/dates: article says Mutaguchi's superior Kawabe vetoed the 8 April move to Dimapur; left out for length.
The article says the siege began on 6 April but the lead says Japanese attacks began 3 April and the battle 4 April; both are reflected.
